title: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “What Perception and Analysis Do” (from p. 548), p. 550. Scope: inference of generating rules from the output of cellular automata and other simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The comparative difficulty is directly benchmarkable on broad public rule collections. The words 'often' and 'general' require a distribution over programs, so results remain conditional on the chosen benchmark.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate held-out outputs from enumerated simple programs and measure rule-recovery accuracy and computational cost for inference methods, stratified by output complexity and compared with traditional mathematical families. Lower recovery despite matched rule length would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No finite benchmark represents all general simple programs.

Difficulty depends on the prior over rules and observation length.

Some inference problems are formally unidentifiable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data existence: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.58
operationalizability: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For elementary cellular automata the outputs are trivial to generate and the rule space is finite, so inversion difficulty can be measured now for that class. Traditional low-complexity rules are the natural control, and they are often easy to guess. The claim's scope is 'general simple programs', which is larger than any one finished survey.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Generate output from a declared class of simple programs, give standard inference methods only the output, and measure how often they recover the rule within a resource bound. Frequent recovery would refute 'extremely difficult'; recovery only for traditionally simple rules, and failure on complex-output rules, would support the contrast.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
There is no algorithm that inverts arbitrary programs, so the result depends on the size cutoff of the search.

'Extremely difficult' needs a cost threshold.
